body.text: [1,1 : Affe und Keil]
body.translated_text: [1,1: The Monkey and the Wedge]

body.text:
asti kaścid vaṇijakaḥ |
nagarasamīpe tena devatāyatanaṃ kriyate |
tatra ye karmakārās sthapatyādayaḥ ! madhyāhnavelāyām
āhāranimittaṃ bhojanamaṇḍapam anupraviṣṭāḥ |
akasmāc cānuṣaṅgikaṃ devagṛhe vānarayūtham āgatam |
atha tatraikasya śilpino 'rdhasphoṭitakāṣṭhastambho
arjunamayaḥ khadirakīlakena madhye yantranikhātenāvastabdho
avatiṣṭhate |
tatra kadācid vānarayūtho giriśikharād avatīrya svecchayā
taruśikharaprāsādaśṛṅgadārunicayeṣu prakrīḍitum ārabdhaḥ |
ekas tu tatrāsannavināśaś cāpalād upaviśya stambhe yantracāram
uddiśyedam āha |
kenāyam asthāne kīlako nikhātaḥ |
iti pāṇibhyām eva saṅgṛhyotpāṭitum ārabdhaḥ |
sthānāc calite kīle yad vṛttam ! tad anākhyeyam ! evam eva bhavatā
jñātam iti |
body.translated_text: There was a certain merchant. Near the town, a temple was being built by him. The workers there — the master-builders and others — at midday, for the purpose of eating, entered the dining hall. By chance, incidentally, a troop of monkeys came to the temple. Now, there was a pillar of <s>arjuna</s> wood, half-split by one of the craftsmen, held open in the middle by a wedge of <s>khadira</s> wood fixed as a device. Once, a troop of monkeys, having descended from the mountain peak, began to frolic at will on the treetops, palace spires, and heaps of timber. But one among them, near to his destruction, out of curiosity sat upon the pillar and, regarding the mechanism, said this: 'Who has fixed this wedge in the wrong place?' Thus, grasping it with both hands, he began to pull it out. When the wedge was dislodged from its place, what happened is unspeakable! Thus it is known to you.

asti kaścid gomāyur āhāravicchedāt kṣutkṣāmakaṇṭha itaś ca
itaḥ paribhramann ubhayasainasyāyodhanabhūmim apaśyat |

śabdaḥ ! kva vā kīdṛśo vaiṣa śabda iti ! cintayatā dṛṣṭā
giriśikharākārā bherī |
tāṃ ca dṛṣṭvācintayat |
kim ayaṃ śabdo 'syās svābhāvikaḥ ! uta paraprerita iti |
atha sā yadā vāyupreritair vṛkṣāgrais spṛśyate ! tadā śabdaṃ karoti !
anyadā na ! iti tūṣṇīm āste |
sa tu tasyās sārāsāratāṃ jñātuṃ saṃnikarṣam upaśliṣṭaḥ |
svayaṃ ca kautukād ubhayor mukhayor atāḍayat ! acintayac ca|
gamyaṃ caitad bhaksyaṃ ca mama |
ity avadhāryaikadaṃṣṭrayā kṣudhāviṣṭaḥ pāṭitavān |
paruṣatvāc ca carmaṇaḥ kathamapi na daṃṣṭrābhaṅgam avāptavān |
pratibaddhāś ca punar apy acintayat |
nūnam asyā antar bhakṣyaṃ bhaviṣyatīti |
ity adhyavasya bheryā mukhaṃ vidāryāntaḥ praviṣṭaḥ |
tasminn api na kiñcid āsāditavān |
pratinivartitum aśakto 'ntarlīnārdhakāyo vihasyābravīt |
pūrvam eva mayā jñātam iti |
body.translated_text: There was a certain jackal, his throat emaciated by hunger due to lack of food, wandering here and there, and he saw the battlefield of two armies. There he heard a great sound. His heart agitated by fear of it, [he thought:] 'What is this? I am destroyed! Whose sound is this? Where, and of what kind, is this sound?' While thinking thus, he saw a drum shaped like a mountain peak. And seeing it, he thought: 'Is this sound natural to it, or is it caused by something else?' When it was touched by tree-branches driven by the wind, it made a sound; otherwise not — and then it was silent. He approached it closely to determine whether it had substance or was hollow. And he himself, out of curiosity, struck both faces [of the drum] and thought: 'This is accessible and is food for me.' Having determined this, driven by hunger, he tore at it with one tooth. But because of the toughness of the leather, he somehow did not break his tooth. Though frustrated, he thought again: 'Surely there will be food inside this.' Having resolved this, he tore open the face of the drum and entered inside. Even there, he found nothing. Unable to return, with half his body stuck inside, he laughed and said: 'I knew it all along!'

body.translated_text: In a certain region, there lived a wandering ascetic (<s>parivrāṭ</s>) named <s>Devaśarmā</s>. Through the accumulation of fine garments obtained from many holy men, he had amassed a great fortune. And he did not trust anyone at all. Now once, a thief of others' wealth named <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s>, thinking 'How can I steal this fortune of his?', approached him in the guise of a devoted attendant and in due course won his trust. Then once, that wandering ascetic, on the occasion of a pilgrimage, set out to travel together with <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s>. And in a certain forest tract, near a riverbank, having stationed <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s> with his belongings, he went alone to fetch water. And he saw a great fight between two rams. Seeing much blood falling to the ground from between the horns of the two [rams], who were endowed with unceasing fighting power, a jackal (<s>gomāyu</s>), its mind bound by hope and greedy for flesh, tried to seize it and, being crushed between their colliding [horns], instantly perished. Then the ascetic, filled with wonder, said: 'The jackal [died] by the rams' fight!' Having completed his ablutions and returned to that spot, <s>Devaśarmā</s> did not see <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s>, who had departed having seized the essence of his wealth. He only saw the discarded triple staff, wooden bowl, strainer, broom, and such [ascetic implements]! And he thought: 'Where is that <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s>? Surely I have been robbed by him!' Thus he spoke: 'And we [were robbed] by <s>Āṣāḍhabhūti</s>!' Then that one, left with only a fragment of a skull-bowl and a knotted cord, entered a certain village at sunset. Upon entering, he saw a weaver living in seclusion and requested lodging. That [weaver] too, having assigned him a place in a part of his own house, told his wife: 'Until I go to the city and, having met my friends and drunk liquor, return — until then, you must remain at home without negligence.' Having instructed her thus, he departed. Now his wife, a loose woman, prompted by a female messenger, adorned herself and set out to go to her lover. But her husband, coming toward her with speech slurred from the effects of intoxication, stumbling in gait, with garments slipping off, arrived [home]. Seeing him, she, being quick-witted, skillfully removed her finery, resumed her former plain appearance, and began attending to his foot-washing, bedding, and other arrangements. The weaver, upon entering the house, fell under the power of sleep. Having slept and awakened, he began to rebuke her: 'Harlot! My friends describe your misdeeds to me. So be it! I shall administer a severe punishment!' She too, being shameless, began to offer retorts. And having awakened again, he tied her firmly to the central pillar with a rope and fell asleep. The messenger urged her to go again. She, being resourceful, tied the messenger in her own place [to maintain the appearance of being bound] and went to her lover. When he awakened again, he began to rebuke her just as before. But the messenger, with a fearful heart, afraid of uttering unfamiliar words, said nothing at all. The weaver, through cunning [thinking] 'She gives me no reply at all,' rose and cut off her nose with a sharp blade, saying: 'Stay just like that, with such a mark! Who will ask about your affairs now?' Having spoken thus, he fell back under the power of sleep. The weaver's wife, having returned, asked the messenger: 'What is your situation? Did he wake and say anything? Tell me, tell me!' The messenger, having been punished, showing her [cut] nose, said angrily: 'All is well with you! Let me go! I am leaving!' And with that done, she took the nose and departed. The weaver's wife also made herself appear as though still tied up, just as before. The weaver, awakening again as before, berated her. But that wicked one spoke far more boldly: 'Shame on you, wretch! Who is able to disfigure me, an innocent woman? Let the world-protectors (<s>lokapālas</s>) hear me! Just as I, apart from my husband since girlhood, do not know another man even in thought — by this truth of mine, may my face remain unblemished!' Then that fool, his mind deluded by her contrived words, lit a torch, and seeing his wife's face unblemished, widened his eyes, kissed her, released her from her bonds with joy, embraced her tightly, and placed her on the bed. The wandering ascetic, from the very beginning, had observed the entire sequence of events as they occurred. The messenger too, with her nose held in her hand, went to her own house and thought: 'What is to be done now?' Then her husband, a barber, coming from the royal court at dawn, said to his wife: 'Hand over the razor-kit, good woman! I have work to do at the royal court.' But she, with evil intentions, standing inside, sent only the razor [not the full kit]. The barber, angered at not receiving the complete razor-kit, sent that very razor back to her in reverse [i.e., blade-first]. Thereupon she uttered a loud cry of pain, wiped her nose with her hand, threw down the nose with its flow of blood onto the ground, and cried: 'Save me! Save me! This man has disfigured me, an innocent woman!' Royal servants who had come, seeing her disfigured as if before their very eyes, severely beat the barber with pegs, heels, and clubs, and then, with his arms bound, the barber was taken along with her to the court of justice. When questioned by the officials — 'Why have you committed this great violence against your own wife?' — and when, though asked repeatedly, he gave no answer, the judges of justice ordered: 'Let him be impaled!' The ascetic, seeing the innocent barber being led to the place of impalement, out of compassion for beings and having ascertained the true facts, approached the court and said to the judges: 'You should not impale this barber, who has committed no offense. For this reason, hear these three wonders!'

body.translated_text: In a certain region there was a tree, and on it a pair of crows lived together. At the time of their breeding, a black serpent, dwelling in the hollow of that very tree, would devour their offspring even before they had begun to act [i.e., while still helpless]. Then, distressed by that harm, [the crow] asked a jackal, his dear friend who dwelt at the base of another tree: 'Good friend, what do you think is appropriate in such a situation? body.translated_text: There is [a story]. A certain crane, due to old age, desiring a livelihood obtained by easy means, stood at a certain lakeside, displaying his own form as if overwhelmed by dejection. There, one crab, surrounded by many fish, said: 'Uncle! Why is your food-gathering activity not being performed today as before?' The crane [replied]: 'I am a fish-eater. But without that pretense, I tell you. Having come to know you previously, I protected your lives. Now, the cessation of my livelihood has arrived. Therefore I am dispirited.' The crab [asked]: 'Uncle! For what reason?' The crane [said]: 'Today, fishermen passing near this lake said: "This lake is full of fish. Let us cast a net into it. There are other lakes near the city that we have not visited. We shall visit them and come back." So, my dears, you are as good as destroyed! And I too, through the cessation of my livelihood, am as good as ruined.' Then they entreated him: 'Since danger is heard of from this very quarter, a remedy too may be found from this very quarter. So please be our protector.' The crane [said]: 'I am egg-born — I am incapable of opposing humans. But I shall transfer you from this lake to another body of water.' Then, having gained confidence, they said: 'Father! Brother! Uncle! Uncle! Take me! Take me! Take me first!' That wicked-minded one, having carried them one by one with skill, continuously devouring them, attained supreme satisfaction. The crab, however, agitated by the fear of death, repeatedly entreated him: 'Uncle! Please be so kind as to rescue even me from the jaws of death.' That evil-souled one thought: 'I am weary of this monotonous fish-flesh. I shall now savor this one as a delicacy of different flavor.' Then, having lifted him up through the air, having avoided all water-places, he descended at a spot on a sun-heated rock. The crab too, having seen the heap of bones and limbs of previously devoured fish, thought thus: 'Those fish have been deliberately slain by this evil-souled one. What then is timely now? However —'

body.translated_text: The crane, though unfamiliar with the crab's pincer-grip, through his own folly met with decapitation from the crab. The crab, having seized the crane's neck like the stalk of a lotus, traveled back by the path marked out for aerial passage, directly toward the fish. And they asked him: 'Brother! Where is that uncle?' Then he replied: 'He has met his end. Here is the head of that evil-souled one. Many of your own kin were devoured by him under false pretense. He too has perished at my hands.' Therefore I say: 'Having devoured many fish...' [the crane met his end]. Then the crow said to the jackal: 'What do you think is the right course of action for us two?' The jackal [replied]: 'Take the golden chain and place it in that dwelling-place [of the snake]. Without doubt, its owner will have that black serpent killed.' Having said this, the jackal departed. Then the crow, searching for a golden chain, went to the royal palace. And he saw, in a section of the inner apartments, placed atop freshly washed garments — a golden chain set with excellent gems, of great value, placed by a maidservant after washing. And she, having set it down, began to converse with another [maid]. The crow, however, having taken it, went through the sky slowly, showing himself, toward his own dwelling. Then the palace guards, wielding spears, clubs, and lances in their hands, went with great speed and examined the tree — and [they found] that the crow had placed it in his own nest. One of them, climbing up, saw a black cobra that, having devoured the crow's chicks, had fallen asleep. And he killed it while it was still sleeping. Having done this, he took the golden chain and departed.

body.translated_text: There is [a story]. In a certain forest-tract, a great lion dwelt. He incessantly slaughtered the deer. Then all the deer together, with bowed hearts, holding green grass-shoots in their mouths, their knees touching the ground, addressed the king of beasts: 'O king of beasts! What is the use of your lord's cruel and needless act of slaughtering all the deer, which is contrary to the interests of the next world? We are destroyed already! And for you too there will be a lack of food. So this is a calamity for both sides. Therefore, be gracious. We shall send to the master, one by one, in turn, a forest-dweller born of our own species.' When this was done, in due course of time, it became the hare's turn. He, commanded by all the deer, thought angrily: 'This entry into the jaws of death is the bringer of my end. What is the right course of action for me now? However — what is impossible for the intelligent? I myself shall slay the lion by a stratagem.' Thus, having let the lion's mealtime pass, he went. That one [the lion], his throat emaciated with hunger, his eyes reddened with anger, his fangs terrible from the grinding of his quivering lips and teeth, causing fear by the manner of his tail-lashing, said to him: 'What is to be done even by the supremely enraged, other than taking away life? You today are as good as dead! What is this delay in your appointed time?' The hare [said]: 'The mealtime has not been missed by me, master, who am under my own control.' The lion [asked]: 'By whom were you detained?' The hare [said]: 'By a lion.' Hearing this, the lion, his heart supremely agitated, said: 'How is there another lion here in this forest protected by my arms?' The hare said: 'Indeed so.' Then the lion reflected: 'What purpose is there in killing this one? He will show me that rival. Having slain that one, I shall devour this one.' Thus he said to him: 'Show me that evil-souled one.' The hare, inwardly laughing, having taken as authoritative the <s>Nītiśāstra</s> (treatise on statecraft) of <s>Bṛhaspati</s> and <s>Uśanas</s>, for the accomplishment of his own purpose, showed him a great well, lined with bricks, filled with clear water, with water reachable [only] at the depth of two men. That one [the lion], not recognizing the reflection of his own body, his mind gone astray, thinking 'This is that rival,' leaped suddenly upon it from above, and through his own folly met his end.

body.translated_text: A certain king had a bed endowed with all excellent qualities, unmatched by any other. In a corner of the coverlet of that bed dwelt a louse named <s>Mandavisarpiṇī</s> (Slow-crawler). Then a bedbug named <s>Ṭiṇṭibha</s>, driven by the wind, fell upon that bed. Seeing that bed with its extremely fine coverlet, pillows on both sides, as wide as the sand-banks of the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Ganges), supremely soft and fragrant, he was filled with extreme delight. With his mind attracted by its touch, wandering about here and there in thought, somehow he met <s>Mandavisarpiṇī</s>. She said to him: 'From where have you come to this unfit dwelling place? Go away from here!' The bedbug said: 'Noble lady! I have tasted here many kinds of flesh and the blood dwelling within <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, <s>kṣatriyas</s>, <s>vaiśyas</s>, and <s>śūdras</s>. But they were rough, slimy, unsatisfying, and unpleasant. But the blood of the master of this bed will surely be delightful, like <s>amṛta</s> (nectar). Constantly attended by physicians with medicines and remedies to control <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣma</s> (phlegm), in a state of health, his blood is nourished by smooth and tender liquids, dishes rich with raw sugar, jaggery, pomegranate, the three pungent spices, and strengthened with the finest meats of creatures of land, water, and sky — I regard it as an elixir of life. And I wish, by your grace, to taste that fragrant and nourishing [blood].' Then <s>Mandavisarpiṇī</s> said: 'This is impossible for those of your kind, who have fiery mouths and the habits of biting flies. Go away from this bed!' Then he fell at her feet. She, out of courtesy, assented: 'Very well.' 'But you must not bite him at an improper time or on too tender a spot.' He said: 'What is the proper time? I do not know, being unfamiliar.' She said: 'When he is drowsy from the fatigue of drinking honey-wine, or deeply asleep from the exhaustion of amorous play — then you should gently and softly explore [his blood]. With his body overcome by the sleep of intoxication and fatigue, he will not quickly awaken.' But having been thus instructed, at the very first watch of the night, not knowing the proper time, [the bedbug] bit [the king]. That king too, as if burned by a firebrand, clutching his belly area, rising in alarm, said: 'Alas! I have been bitten by something!' Then the bedbug, in fright upon hearing the king's words, descended from the bed and took refuge in another crevice. But when the bed-attendants, searching skillfully by the master's command, turned over the cloth, they found <s>Mandavisarpiṇī</s> hiding within, and killed her.

body.translated_text: Near a certain city, there lived in a nearby burrow a jackal named <s>Caṇḍarava</s> (Fierce-howler). Once, searching for food, having reached nightfall, his throat parched with hunger, eyes half-closed, wandering about, he entered the city. The dogs dwelling in that city, tearing his limbs with the tips of their sharp teeth — filling the quarters with fearsome cries of terror, stumbling here and there while fleeing, he unknowingly fell into a vat of indigo dye. The pack of dogs departed the way they had come. He too, with difficulty, having some life remaining, emerged from that indigo vat. Then, seeing his body dyed with indigo color, the nearby jackals, [wondering] 'Who is this?', with eyes trembling in fear, fled in all directions. He too reflected: 'Surely, seeing this transformation of my form, they are fleeing.' Then, with a steady mind, he slowly addressed them: 'Enough of this alarm! I have come to the earth by the command of <s>Ākhaṇḍala</s> (Indra), capable of protecting all the clans of wild animals.' Then, hearing his words, the lions, tigers, panthers, monkeys, rabbits, deer, bulls, gadflies, jackals, and other groups of wild animals bowed to him. And every day, with his belly filled with the flesh of mighty elephants torn open by the claws of lions, tusks of boars, and thunderbolts — keeping that pack of jackals outside like a thicket, he made the lions, tigers, and others his close attendants. But one day, his hunger satisfied with various meats, hearing the howling cries of jackals standing in the various directions, he hastily howled aloud. Thereupon, those lions and others, looking at the ground in shame, [said:] 'Alas! We have been deceived! This is a jackal!' — having ascertained this, in anger they destroyed that harsh-voiced one.

body.translated_text: In a certain forest region, there lived a lion named <s>Madotkaṭa</s> (Rut-fierce). He had three attendants who were meat-eaters: a panther, a crow, and a jackal. Once, while roaming, they saw a camel that had strayed from a caravan. Seeing its unfamiliar form, which provoked laughter, the lion asked: 'This is an unusual creature here in the forest. Let it be asked: Who are you?' Then the crow, having ascertained the truth, said: 'This is a camel, as its name indicates.' Then, having won its confidence, they brought it before the lion. The camel told him the true account of how it had been separated from the caravan. The lion gave it refuge and a grant of fearlessness. While things continued thus, once the lion, his body wounded by the tusks of a wild elephant in battle, became confined to his cave. When five or six days had passed, all of them fell into a desperate state from lack of food. As they grew weak, the lion addressed them: 'I am unable, with this pain, to procure food for you as before. You should make an effort on your own behalf.' They said to him: 'In this situation, what concern do we have for our own nourishment?' The lion said: 'Your conduct as loyal followers and your devotion to me are excellent. Most commendable words. You are capable, and I am ailing. Therefore, bring food to me in this condition.' But when they said nothing, he addressed them: 'What is this shame? Let some creature be sought. Even in this condition, I will procure sustenance for you and for myself.' Having been told this, they rose and entered the deeper forest together with <s>Krathanaka</s> [the camel]. Having set <s>Krathanaka</s> aside, they began their evil counsel. The crow said: 'We are being destroyed by this master, even in a matter within our own power.' The other two said: 'How so?' He said: 'Is it not this <s>Krathanaka</s> [who should be our food]?' They said: 'This one has come to us seeking refuge in trust and has been accepted as a friend. He is protected by the master with a grant of fearlessness.' [The crow said:] 'Grass-eaters and meat-eaters make incompatible companions.' The other two said: 'This is improper and impossible, since the master protects him.' Again the crow said: 'You stay here — I myself will accomplish this purpose.' Having said this, he went to the lion. The lion asked: 'Have you found some creature?' The crow said: 'Let whoever has eyes or strength go search. We are all blind from lack of food and our strength is exhausted. But there is something that must necessarily be communicated in due time. The master has destroyed himself by his own self, even in a matter within his own power.' The lion said: 'How so?' The crow said: 'Is it not this <s>Krathanaka</s>?' The lion said: 'Terrible! This is cruel! I have given him refuge and a grant of fearlessness. Moreover —'

body.translated_text: And again he said: 'Let the master not kill it himself. The killing of this one has been started by me through a stratagem.' The lion [asked]: 'How so?' The crow [said]: 'This one, seeing the master in this condition and us, will himself offer his own body for the nourishment of others, for going to heaven, and for the welfare of beings.' When the crow had spoken thus, the lion, as if thrown into mental confusion, said nothing at all. And he, going to them again, informed each one with contrived words: 'Having gone before the lion, you must speak thus.' Then, having made their agreement, they went together with <s>Krathanaka</s> (the camel) to the lion. Then the crow, having bowed, addressed the lion: 'Lord! The master's body must be protected at all costs with our own bodies.' Then he [the lion] said: 'Your body is insufficient. Even if your body were consumed, it would cause no satisfaction for us.' And when he had withdrawn, the jackal said: 'My body is more substantial than theirs. So let the master's life be sustained by my life.' Him too he addressed in the same way. And when he had withdrawn, the leopard said: 'My body is more substantial than theirs — let it be used.' Him too he [the lion] said: 'Your body too is insufficient.' Hearing that, <s>Krathanaka</s> thought: 'None of them is being destroyed here. So I too shall speak in the same way.' Then, rising and approaching the lion, he said: 'Lord! My body is more substantial than theirs. Therefore, let the master's life be sustained by my body.' Even as he was speaking thus, the leopard and the jackal tore open both his flanks, and he instantly died and was devoured.

body.translated_text: In a certain lake lived a tortoise named <s>Kambugrīva</s> (Conch-Neck). He had two friends, geese named <s>Vikaṭa</s> and <s>Saṃkaṭa</s>. In an adverse turn of time, a twelve-year drought occurred. Then they both thought: 'This lake has diminished water. Let us go to another body of water. But let us take leave of our dear friend <s>Kambugrīva</s>, with whom we have long resided.' When they did so, the tortoise said to them: 'Why are you merely taking leave of me? If there is affection, then you ought to save me too from this mouth of death. For you two, there is merely a lack of food in this lake of little water; but for me here, it is death itself. So consider: which is worse — loss of food or loss of a friend?' They said: 'You speak rightly. It is so. But do you know what is appropriate to the moment? We will certainly carry you. But you must not say anything out of restlessness. Hold this stick in the middle with your teeth. Thus, lifted by this very means, we will carry you sixty <s>yojanas</s> to a great lake. There we shall live happily.' And when this was accomplished, seeing him being carried above the city near that lake, the people became a great commotion: 'What is this thing the size of a cart-wheel being carried through the sky?' And hearing that, the tortoise, near to his destruction, letting go of the stick, said: 'I am a tortoise!' Speaking thus from restlessness — 'These people are babbling!' — at the very moment of his speech, having fallen from his support, he fell to the ground, and at the very moment of his fall, the people, eager for meat, cut him to pieces with sharp blades.

body.translated_text: In a certain great lake lived three large fish, namely: <s>Anāgatavidhātā</s> (Provider-against-the-Future), <s>Pratyutpannamati</s> (Present-Minded), and <s>Yadbhaviṣya</s> (What-Will-Be-Will-Be). Once, <s>Anāgatavidhātā</s>, while inside the water, heard the words of fishermen passing nearby: 'This lake has many fish. Let us fish here.' Hearing that, <s>Anāgatavidhātā</s> thought: 'They will surely come. So I, taking <s>Pratyutpannamati</s> and <s>Yadbhaviṣya</s>, shall resort to another lake with an unobstructed outlet.' Then, having summoned those two, he asked them to depart. There, <s>Pratyutpannamati</s>, dissuaded by [his own] judgment and confident of safety, somehow out of negligence did not follow. But <s>Yadbhaviṣya</s>, near to his destruction, disregarding those words, remained completely inactive. The next day, after <s>Anāgatavidhātā</s> had departed, the fishermen blocked the inner outlet and cast the all-encompassing net. And when the net was drawn, not a single one remained in that lake. In this situation, <s>Pratyutpannamati</s>, assuming the appearance of a dead fish, displayed himself on the surface of the water. They, thinking 'A large fish has died by itself,' placed him in the side-stream. From there, having leaped out, he went to another body of water. But <s>Yadbhaviṣya</s>, his body battered by numerous blows of clubs, was led to death. Therefore I say: '<s>Anāgatavidhātā</s>...' and so on. Now, once, when the female <s>ṭīṭibhī</s> had laid [her eggs], the ocean, to test her husband, carried away those eggs, [thinking:] 'Let me see what this one undertakes!' Then the female <s>ṭīṭibhī</s>, seeing the nest empty, with her heart in utmost distress, said to her husband: 'This is what has befallen me, the unfortunate one!' He, suppressing his inner laughter, said to her: 'Dear one, let my ability also be seen!' Then, having assembled a gathering of birds, he reported the grief caused by the taking of his offspring. One among them said: 'We are incapable of fighting the great ocean. What then is appropriate here? All of us together, by our cries, shall alarm <s>Garutmān</s> (<s>Garuḍa</s>). He alone will take away our grief.' Having resolved this, they went to him. And <s>Garuḍa</s>, who had been summoned by <s>Viṣṇu</s> for a battle of gods and demons, seeing the distress of his own kind, became angry. And Lord <s>Viṣṇu</s>, due to his capacity of seeing the three times, knowing what was in his heart, himself went to him. Then, seeing the Lord, [<s>Garuḍa</s>], his heart all the more agitated, said: 'It is fitting that you, being the protector, [should address] this insult done to me by that wretch, the ocean!' And the Lord, having understood, laughingly said this to the ocean: 'Return the offspring of the <s>ṭīṭibha</s> at once! Otherwise I shall quickly render you, scorched by the fire-weapon, depleted of water through many thousands of submarine fire-mouths.' Thus addressed, the great ocean thought: 'Total destruction has been begun by one born of my own egg [i.e., <s>Garuḍa</s>].' Thinking thus, he bowed to the Lord and returned [the eggs].

body.translated_text: In a certain forest region, a lion named <s>Vajradanta</s> (Diamond-tooth) lived together with a wolf, a jackal, and a camel. Once, his chest torn by the tusk of a wild elephant, stationed in one place, his body emaciated with hunger, he said to those ministers who had come [to him] out of hunger: 'Search for some creature in the forest! So that I, even in this condition, may provide your livelihood.' Then, at the very moment of that command, they wandered in the forest, and when they found nothing, that jackal spoke privately to the camel named <s>Śaṅkukarṇa</s> (Spike-ear): 'What do you think is appropriate here? Our lord <s>Vajradanta</s>, hearing that our wandering has been fruitless, may at some point turn to [our] destruction. Therefore I request something of you — if you would agree.' He said: 'What do I have, friend, that could be asked for? Even my body is at your disposal. Use it as you wish.' Then the jackal said: 'That is exactly the thing [needed] here. I shall have the lion give you a body twice the size [of yours].' [He added:] 'And by this, we and you yourself will be sustained.' And the other agreed. Having said this, [the jackal] went to the lion and told him: 'Lord! No creature has been found. But this <s>Śaṅkukarṇa</s> says: I shall give over my body [to be weighed] by a double scale against the large measure (<s>bṛhatprastha</s>).' Hearing this, the lion, delighted, said: 'So be it!' Then, when the agreement was made, <s>Śaṅkukarṇa</s> fell to the ground and was cut to pieces. Then the clever one [i.e. the jackal], seeing the lion with his entire body smeared with blood, said: 'Let our lord go to perform his bath, while I remain here together with <s>Kravyamukha</s> (Flesh-face, the wolf).' When that one had gone, the clever one said to <s>Kravyamukha</s>: 'Eat some of this flesh quickly, while he has gone to bathe!' He said: 'If I eat, what answer shall I give?' The jackal said: 'What is the point of such deliberation? I shall give the answer for this. You need only look at my face [for a signal].' When it was thus agreed, the two of them ate a great deal of the flesh. Meanwhile, the lion returned, and when he saw that all the belly-flesh had been consumed, he said to the clever one: 'Dear one! Where is that belly-flesh?' While the lion was speaking thus, <s>Kravyamukha</s> looked at the face of the clever one. The clever one said: 'Why do you now look at my face? Lord! It was eaten by this one!' Then the lion, with claws sharp as a thunderbolt, with brows knitted and face [showing] manifest rage, wished to kill him. And that wolf too, his body seized by pallor of face and trembling, his steps extended to great strides, swift in rapid flight, fled toward the deep forest. The lion too, having pursued for a little while, turned back. In the meantime, by some chance, a certain caravan-leader came by this very path near that spot. Seeing the caravan's lead camel approaching with a bowl tied to its neck, the jackal, feigning distress, said to the lion: 'Lord! We are both destroyed! Let no one [else] possess the forest! Just when even now the flesh has not been consumed, this little camel has arrived with the large measure, in the manner of a creditor [demanding repayment]. What is appropriate here? Let our lord go to another direction, while I render this one well-disposed in mind.' When this was said, the lion departed from there. And the clever one feasted on that flesh for many days.

body.translated_text: In a certain forest region, there was a great troop of monkeys. Once, in the winter season, sitting uncomfortably, with extreme agitation, seeing a firefly and thinking 'This is fire,' [a monkey] covered it with dry grass, leaves, and other fuel, extended his arms, and experienced — so they say — the imagined pleasure of warmth, scratching his armpits, belly, and chest. One particular monkey there, his mind fixed on that [firefly], blew on it again and again with his mouth. Then a bird named <s>Sūcīmukha</s> (Needle-beak), having descended from the tree, said to him: 'Don't trouble yourself! This is not fire — this is a firefly.' But he kept blowing, disregarding that one's words entirely. And though warned repeatedly, he did not stop at all. In short — that one [the bird], coming close to his ear again and again, persistently annoyed him, until [the monkey], suddenly seizing him and dashing him against a rock, killed him.

body.translated_text: In a certain town, there were two merchant's sons who were friends. One was <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> (Wicked-wit) and the other <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> (Righteous-wit). The two went to a distinguished foreign land for the purpose of earning wealth. There, the one named <s>Dharmabuddhi</s>, the caravan-leader's son, prompted by his own good fortune, obtained a thousand silver <s>dīnāras</s> stored in a pot that had been deposited long ago by some good man. Having deliberated with <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> — 'Now that we have succeeded, let us return to our own country' — the two returned. Near the town, <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> said: 'Let the <s>dīnāras</s> be divided in half shares. Let us enter our homes. Now we shall live splendidly in the presence of friends and relatives.' But <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s>, hard-hearted within, said to him for his own advantage: 'Good friend! As long as the remaining wealth is held in common between us, our bond of affection continues unbroken. Rather, let us each take one hundred and enter. The reason is: the testing of our merit will happen through decrease and increase, and the unity of [our shared] purpose will be enviable to people.' When this was done accordingly, they hid the remainder in some well-concealed place and entered [the town]. Then, within that year, <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s>, being addicted to wasteful expenditure and due to a gap in his fortune, exhausted his share and once again went with <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> to divide another hundred from the deposit. That too was likewise exhausted within the second year. Things being thus, <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> thought: 'If we divide again in portions of one hundred, what will that amount to for me? If I steal the remaining six [hundred], I shall obtain everything.' Having decided thus, going alone, he removed that entire fortune, leveled the spot, and after a month had passed, said to <s>Dharmabuddhi</s>: 'Friend! Make an equal division of the remaining wealth.' When <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> agreed and they went together to that very place and began to dig, and when nothing was found in the digging, <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> was the first to boldly strike his own head with a stone and said in agitation: 'Where is that [wealth], O <s>Brahman</s>-hearted one! <s>Dharmabuddhi</s>! Surely you have stolen it!' Thus disputing with mutual suspicion, the two came to the court of justice. When the matter was reported and understood, since the case with unclear evidence was difficult to resolve, [the proceedings] were adjourned. Within five days, <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> declared to the officials: 'I have witnesses regarding the <s>dīnāras</s> in this dispute.' They asked him, for the purpose of settling the case: 'Who is your witness? Show [them].' He said: 'The very tree under which the money was deposited — by that [tree] I shall prove it.' At this they were astonished — 'How will a tree testify?' — and having taken surety from both, sent them home. Then <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s>, having gone to his own home, said to his father: 'Father! Those stakes are in my hands. But they rest solely on a verbal [guarantee]. Today at night I shall place you in the hollow of this tree. At dawn, when asked in the presence of the judges of justice, give testimony against him.' Then [the father] said: 'Son! We are both destroyed! Why? This is a scheme without [proper] means.' body.translated_text: There is [a story]. In a certain <s>arjuna</s> tree, a pair of cranes lived. And there, a great-bodied serpent, frequenting the hollow of the tree, would devour the offspring even before they had begun to act [i.e., while still helpless]. Through that despair, the two, having lost their senses, abandoning their feeding activity, sat dejected at one side of the lake. Then a certain crab there said to him: 'Uncle! Is feeding still not being done today?' The crane [said]: 'For me, overcome by despondency, whence would come a desire for food?' Thereupon he asked: 'From what sort of cause has this despondency arisen?' He then told him the entire account of the devouring of his offspring as it had occurred. But the crab counseled him: 'I shall tell you the means for killing it. From this mongoose-dwelling, let fish-flesh be scattered in an unbroken line all the way to the serpent's dwelling. Then they will kill it.' When this was done accordingly, the mongooses, following the trail of flesh, remembering their old enmity, cutting the serpent to pieces, running along the path they had previously seen, went to the crane's dwelling and devoured the crane's remaining offspring as well.

body.translated_text: Therefore I say: 'The wise man should think of the expedient, but should also think of the reverse outcome.' Even while saying this, that one was taken by him and placed in the hollow of the tree. Then at dawn, the tree, having been made to speak the words of <s>dharmaśāstra</s> audibly in the presence of the court officials, said as planned: 'The wealth was stolen by <s>Dharmabuddhi</s>.' Hearing that, <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> thought: 'How can a downward-facing tree utter speech? There must be a reason for this. In any case, this can be resolved by intelligence.' Then he addressed the judges: 'What a marvel! Even today my reputation as <s>Dharmabuddhi</s> remains intact in the world. Having come alone to this solitary forest, I took that property. Then I saw a huge serpent approaching. I thought: "What a calamity has befallen!" And I said: "Objects can be obtained again, but not life. I shall come again." Thus I deposited it at the very root of this tree. Now it must be handed over by royal command. But please stand at a distance from this spot while I vanquish this black serpent, the guardian of the treasure.' Having said this, having filled the tree-hollow with dry wood, leaves, and other combustible materials, he began to set fire [to it]. But <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s>, looking down from the corner of his eye and seeing the merchant's son inside the tree-hollow, became distressed in mind. When the fire was lit and the tree-hollow was blazing all around, the merchant's son, with body cracked, hair singed, and skin peeling off, fell to the ground. Seeing that great commotion, they were filled with supreme wonder, [thinking] 'What is this?' And perceiving that the merchant's son was still barely alive, they asked him: 'What is this fire-fall that has befallen you?' Then he said: 'By this wicked son [<s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s>] I have been brought to this state.' Speaking thus, he perished. Thereupon the judges of justice, having learned the truth, declared: 'Let this sinful <s>Duṣṭabuddhi</s> be impaled!'

body.translated_text: There is [a story]. In a certain town, a merchant's son who had lost his relatives [lived]. He set out for another country for the purpose of earning wealth. He had a balance made of a thousand [measures of] iron. Having deposited it with another merchant's son, he went to another country to earn wealth. And due to his ill fortune, even after a long time, he gained nothing. Having returned, he requested the balance from him. And that one said: 'It was eaten by mice.' Then he thought: 'This is amazing! How could mice eat a balance made of a thousand [measures of] iron?' Laughing inwardly, he said: 'It must indeed be so! For what reason would rats not eat iron that is virile, sweet, and soft?' — thus he spoke agreeably. That one too, with a very pleased heart, began to offer him worship with foot-washing and the like, and invited him to dine. Not far away was a river. When that one set out to bathe there, he sent his own son, equipped with myrobalan and bathing cloth, behind him. That one too, upon returning, having hidden the boy well in a friend's house, entered. Then at mealtime, the merchant, not seeing the boy, with agitated mind and suspicious heart, asked him: 'Where is that boy who was sent to follow you? He has not entered here.' Then he said: 'He was carried off by a hawk.' Hearing that, extremely distressed and having become merciless, he seized him by the arm and took him to the court of justice, and said: 'Save me! By this man my son has been hidden somewhere.' When questioned by the judges — 'What is this? Speak!' — he laughed and said: 'He was carried off by a hawk.' Then they, with amazed minds, said: 'How could a hawk carry off a boy?' When asked for the truth by the judges, he said: 'What is surprising in this? Where a balance of a thousand [measures of] iron belonging to me was eaten by mice in this man's house, how could a boy not be carried off by a hawk there?' Having heard this, the judges arranged the mutual exchange — the balance for the boy.

body.translated_text: There is, in the southern country, a city called <s>Mihilāropya</s>. Not far from it was a dwelling of wandering ascetics (<s>parivrājakas</s>). There, a wandering ascetic named <s>Jūṭakarṇa</s> lived. At begging time, from that city, being a holy person, from the houses of <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, having filled his begging bowl with special foods containing sugar-candy, molasses, and pomegranate seeds — rich, soft, and delicious — returning to that dwelling and performing his observances in due manner, he stored the remainder carefully in a container and placed it on a wall-peg. [The mouse-narrator says:] 'I, together with my retinue, lived on that. Though it was stored with great care, when it was being eaten [by me], he, dismayed, kept moving it from place to place, higher and higher, out of fear of me. But even that I reached effortlessly and ate. Then, as time went on, once a visiting ascetic named <s>Bṛhatsphij</s> came to him. That <s>Jūṭakarṇa</s>, having offered him welcome and other courtesies, having performed his usual observances, having stored the remainder carefully in that container, sitting on his cot, asked <s>Bṛhatsphij</s> who had gone to bed: "You parted from me here. From then on, in what other countries or ascetic groves have you wandered?" He replied: "Once, at the great <s>Kārttikī</s> festival, having bathed at the excellent holy place of <s>Puṣkara</s>, due to the crush of the great crowd, I was separated from you. Then I, wandering along the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Ganges) — upstream and downstream — through <s>Gaṅgādvāra</s>, <s>Prayāga</s>, <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, and other places — in short, I have seen the entire surface of the earth up to the ocean." While the tale was half-told, the ascetic <s>Jūṭakarṇa</s>, leaning on the wall-peg, repeatedly struck the worn-out [container]. When the interruption of the narrative was thus being made, the angered <s>Bṛhatsphij</s> said: "I, having shown you respect, am telling you my story! But why this disrespect from you?" And thus:

body.translated_text: There is [a story]. Once, when the rainy season was approaching, I requested a certain <s>brāhmaṇa</s> for lodging at some place for the purpose of staying during the rains. When the rainy season had passed, awakened in the last watch of the night for the purpose of travel, I pondered: 'In which direction should I go?' body.translated_text: Therefore I say: 'One should always save...' So, <s>brāhmaṇī</s>! One lives by being resourceful. And when it was pointed out, he began the work of digging. Now I [the mouse <s>Hiraṇyaka</s>], from the very beginning, having heard the private conversation of those two, had abandoned my food and remained standing, full of curiosity. But when he began to search for the burrow, then I realized: 'This evil-souled one has discovered the entrance to my den!' Now, I had obtained gold previously deposited by some good person. Through the power of that [gold], I considered myself mighty. That wicked one, having followed the burrow, found and seized the wealth, and having obtained it again, settled down and said to <s>Jūṭakarṇa</s>: 'This is his treasure-heart [store of wealth], by the power of which he leaps to places even impossible [to reach].' And having divided it in half, they sat comfortably. Having met with my own downfall, I thought: 'Someday, when I am here [in my den], they will light a lamp and, finding me without doubt, kill me.' Therefore, from that place I made another stronghold-place. And the others, my followers, came and said to me: 'Good <s>Hiraṇya</s>! We who dwell near you are extremely afflicted by hunger. We do not have even a morsel of food. Even though the day has ended, we have obtained nothing. So please be kind enough to feed us today at least.' Having said 'Very well,' I went to the dwelling together with them. Standing in seclusion, I heard the rest of the conversation of those two evil-souled ones, previously narrated. Now <s>Jūṭakarṇa</s> was shaking his bamboo stick just as before while telling the story. He [the visitor] said to him: 'Why do you keep shaking the bamboo stick even now, when that one has been dealt with? Stay still! Enough!' Thereupon he replied: 'Good sir! This mouse who harms me comes again and again.' He [the visitor], laughing, said: 'Do not fear! This is nothing. Because —'

body.text:
[ bhavaty arthena balavān arthād bhavati paṇḍitaḥ |
paśyemaṃ mūṣakaṃ pāpaṃ svajātisamatāṃ gatam || 51 || ]
body.translated_text: ['One becomes powerful through wealth; through wealth one becomes wise. Behold this wicked mouse, now reduced to equality with his own kind. || 51 ||]'

body.text:
api ca |
yad asyotpatane śaktikāraṇam ! tad āvayor eva hastagatam |
ahaṃ tu tathaiva samarthitavān |
satyam āhāyam |
na mamādyāṅkulakasyāpy utpatane śaktir astīti |
śṛṇomi cānucarāṇāṃ parasparālāpam |
āgacchata ! gacchāmaḥ |
nāyam adya tṛṇasyāpi kubjīkaraṇe samarthaḥ |
evam uktvā pañcāśanmātrā gatāḥ ! punar api pañcaviṃśatiḥ ! daśa
pañca ceti ! athānye dvādaśāṣṭau |
athāvaśiṣṭau dvau |
tatrāpy eko 'bravīt |
ayam ātmano 'py udarabharaṇe na samarthaḥ ! kiṃ punar anyeṣām |
ity uktvā nirapekṣo 'sāv api prāyāt |
tato 'haṃ paricintyaitavad iti svam ālayaṃ gataḥ |
prabhātasamaye sarvae eva sapatnasakāśaṃ gatāḥ ! daridro 'sāv iti
vadantaḥ |
tathā pravṛttānām anucarāṇām eko 'pi na matsakāśam āgacchat |
paśyāmi ca ! māṃ dṛṣṭvā sammukhaṃ tae eva matsapatnais saha
parasparaṃ kilakilāyanto hastāsphālanair mamānucarās saṅkrīḍanti
sma |
cintitaṃ ca mayā ! yathā |
evam etat |
body.translated_text: Moreover: 'The means that caused his [the mouse's] leaping power — that is now in the hands of us two alone.' I confirmed this as well. He [the mouse] truly said: 'I today do not even have the power to make a fingertip jump!' And I hear the mutual conversation of my followers: 'Come! Let us go! This one today is not even capable of bending a blade of grass.' Having spoken thus, about fifty departed; then another twenty-five; ten; five; then twelve others; [and] eight. Then two remained. Of those, one said: 'This one is not even capable of filling his own belly — let alone feeding others!' Having spoken thus, that one too departed, unconcerned. Then I, having reflected on all this, went to my own dwelling. At dawn, every single one of them went to my rival's side, saying 'He is a pauper!' And of the followers who had thus turned, not even one came to me. And I see this: upon seeing me face-to-face, those very followers of mine, together with my rivals, play about with one another, laughing aloud and clapping hands! And I thought: this is how it is!

body.text:
[ yasyārthās tasya mitrāṇi yasyārthās tasya bāndhavāḥ |
yasyārthās sa pumāṃl loke yasyārthās sa ca paṇḍitaḥ || 52 || ]
body.translated_text: [Whoever has wealth has friends; whoever has wealth has relatives; whoever has wealth is a man in the world; whoever has wealth — he is called a wise man. // 52]

children.text: api ca |
children.translated_text: Moreover:

children.text: [ arthena hi vihīnasya puruṣasyālpamedhasaḥ |
children.translated_text: [For a man bereft of wealth, of little intelligence,

children.text: vicchidyante kriyās sarvā grīṣme kusaritoyathā || 53 ||
children.translated_text: all activities are cut off — like the waters of a river in summer. // 53

children.text: tyajanti mitrāṇi dhanair vihīnaṃ
children.translated_text: Friends abandon one bereft of wealth,

children.text: putrāś ca dārāś ca suhṛjjanāś ca |
children.translated_text: sons and wives and well-wishers too;

children.text: tam arthavantaṃ punar āśrayante |
children.translated_text: but they resort to him again when he has wealth —

children.text: artho hi loke puruṣasya bandhuḥ || 54 ||
children.translated_text: for wealth is truly a man's kinsman in this world. // 54

children.text: daridrasya manuṣyasya prājñasya madhurasya ca |
children.translated_text: A poor man, even if wise and sweet-spoken —

children.text: kāle 'py uktaṃ vākyaṃ na kaścit pratipadyate || 55 ||
children.translated_text: even when his words are timely, no one accepts them. // 55

children.text: caṇḍālaś ca daridraś ca dvāv etau sadṛśau matau |
children.translated_text: An outcaste (<s>caṇḍāla</s>) and a pauper — these two are considered alike;

children.text: caṇḍālasya na gṛhṇanti daridro na prayacchati || 56 ||
children.translated_text: people do not accept from the outcaste, and the pauper does not give. // 56

children.text: arthena parihīṇaṃ tu naram aspṛśyatāṃ gatam |
children.translated_text: A man bereft of wealth, reduced to untouchability —

children.text: tyajanti bāndhavās sarve mṛtaṃ sattvam ivāsavaḥ || 57 ||
children.translated_text: all relatives abandon him, like the vital breaths [abandon] a dead being. // 57

children.text: arthena hīnaḥ puruṣas tyajyate mitrabāndhavaiḥ |
children.translated_text: A man bereft of wealth is abandoned by friends and relatives;

children.text: tyaktalokakriyādāraḥ parāsur iva niṣprabhaḥ || 58 ||
children.translated_text: deprived of worldly rites and wife, he is like one already dead, devoid of luster. // 58

children.text: śūnyam aputrasya gṛhaṃ ciraśūnyaṃ yasya nāsti sanmitram |
children.translated_text: Empty is the house of one without a son; long-empty [is the life] of one without a true friend;

children.text: mūrkhasya diśaś śūnyās sarvaṃ śūnyaṃ daridrasya || 59 ||
children.translated_text: empty are all directions for a fool; everything is empty for a pauper. // 59

body.text:
[ uttiṣṭha kṣaṇam ekam udvaha sakhe dāridryabhāraṃ guruṃ
kliṣṭo yāvad ahaṃ ciraṃ maraṇajaṃ seve tvadīyaṃ sukham |
ity ukto dhanavarjitena viduṣā gatvā śmaśāne śavo
dāridryān maraṇaṃ varaṃ sukhakaraṃ jñātvā sa tūṣṇīṃ sthitaḥ
|| 60 || ]]
body.translated_text: [Rise for just a moment, bear up, O friend, this heavy burden of poverty — while I, long-suffering, enjoy the pleasure of your death. Thus addressed by a destitute learned man [upon going] to a cremation ground, the corpse, knowing that poverty makes death preferable and pleasant, remained silent. // 60]]

body.text:
kim aparaṃ bhoḥ |
na kaścid anyaḥ prativacanam api dadāti |
body.translated_text: What more, O sir? No one else even gives a reply.

body.text:
[ tānīndriyāṇy avikalāni tad eva nāma
sā buddhir apratihatā vacanaṃ tad eva |
arthoṣmaṇā virahitaḥ puruṣas sa eva
śete hakāra iva saṅkucitākhilāṅgaḥ || 61 || ]
body.translated_text: [Those very sense-organs, unimpaired; that same name; that same undiminished intellect; those same words — yet the man deprived of the warmth of wealth lies contracted in all his limbs, like the letter 'ha.' // 61]

body.text:
tat prāyaśo loke svarūpam īdṛśam |
vinipatitam āryam api janaṃ dṛṣṭvā dhany- andho mūkaś ca bhavati
dhanamadāvalepāt |
tathā ca |
body.translated_text: So, for the most part, this is the nature of things in the world. Even seeing a noble person who has fallen, the rich one, blinded and mute with the insolence of wealth-pride, [shows no compassion]. And thus:

body.text:
[ vilocane cāvikale ca vīkṣate
sphuṭā ca vāg asti na cāpabhāṣaṇam |
aho nṛśaṃsair vibhavais tathā kṛtaṃ
yatheśvaro yācanayantratāṃ gataḥ || 62 || ]
body.translated_text: [The eyes are unimpaired and he sees; speech is clear and there is no defect of language — yet, alas, wealth has so cruelly acted that the lord has been reduced to the state of a supplicant. // 62]

body.text:
tan mādṛśānāṃ kiṃ nāma tad varaṃ syāt ! yasya syād īdṛśaḥ
phalavipākaḥ ! yat satataṃ dehīti vakti |
tat sarvathā dhanahīnasya mamādhunā neha śreyaḥ |
uktaṃ ca |
body.translated_text: So, for ones like me, what could be that blessing whose karmic result would be such — that one constantly says 'Give!' Therefore, for me who am now utterly bereft of wealth, there is no welfare here. And it is said:

body.text:
[ vasen mānādhikaṃ sthānaṃ mānahīnaṃ na saṃvaset |
mānahīnaṃ surais sārdhaṃ vimānam api varjayet || 63 || ]
body.translated_text: [One should dwell in a place where honor exceeds; one should not dwell where honor is lacking. A place devoid of honor, even a celestial chariot, one should avoid — even in the company of gods. // 63]

body.text:
evam uktvāpy ahaṃ punar apy evam acintayam |
kimarthitāṃ kasyacit karomi |
tad etat kaṣṭataram |
yatkāraṇam !
body.translated_text: Having spoken thus, I thought again: why should I beg from anyone? That is even more wretched. The reason:

children.text: [ kubjasya kīṭakhātasya dāvaniṣkuṣitatvacaḥ |
children.translated_text: [Of a tree — hump-backed, worm-eaten, bark stripped by fire,

children.text: taror apy ūṣarasthasya varaṃ janma na cārthinaḥ || 64 ||
children.translated_text: standing in barren soil — even its birth is preferable to that of a beggar. // 64

body.text:
kaṇṭhe gadgadatā svedo mukhe vaivarṇyavepathū |
mriyamāṇasya cihnāni yāni tāny eva yācataḥ || 65 || ]
body.translated_text: A choking in the throat, sweat on the face, pallor and trembling — the signs of one who is dying are the same as those of one who begs. // 65]

body.text: tad arthitvam api jaghanyam |
body.translated_text: Therefore, begging too is most despicable.

body.text:
[ vairāgyāharaṇaṃ dhiyo 'paharaṇaṃ mithyāvikalpāspadaṃ
paryāyo maraṇasya dainyavasatiś śaṅkānidhānaṃ param |
mūrtaṃ lāghavam āspadaṃ ca vipadāṃ tejoharaṃ māninām
arthitvaṃ hi manasvināṃ na narakāt paśyāmi vastvantaram || 66 || ]
body.translated_text: [The robbing of dispassion, the stealing of intelligence, the ground of false imaginings, a synonym for death, an abode of wretchedness, a supreme repository of suspicion, embodied degradation, and the foundation of calamities — robbing the luster of the proud — I see nothing in begging other than hell for the self-respecting. // 66]

body.text: api ca |
body.translated_text: Moreover:

body.text:
[ nirdravyo hriyam eti hrīparigataḥ prabhraśyate tejaso
nistejāḥ paribhūyate paribhavān nirvedam āgacchati |
nirviṇṇaś śucam eti śokamanaso buddhiḥ paribhraśyati
nirdhīkaḥ kṣayam ety aho nidhanatā sarvāpadām āspadam || 67 || ]
body.translated_text: [Without wealth, one loses modesty; beset by loss of modesty, one falls from vigor; without vigor, one is insulted; from insult comes despondency; from despondency comes grief; from grief of mind, the intellect is lost; without intellect, one is destroyed — alas, destitution is the abode of all calamities! // 67]

body.text: api ca |
body.translated_text: Moreover:

children.text: [ varam ahimukhe krodhāviṣṭhe karau viniveśitau
children.translated_text: [Better to place one's hands in the mouth of a raging serpent;

children.text: viṣam api varaṃ pītvā suptaṃ yamasya niveśane |
children.translated_text: better to drink poison and sleep in the abode of <s>Yama</s> (Death);

children.text: girivarataṭād ātmā mukto varaṃ śatadhā gato
children.translated_text: better to hurl oneself from a mountain peak and be shattered a hundredfold —

children.text: na tu khalajanāvāptair arthaiḥ priyaṃ kṛtam ātmanaḥ || 68 ||
children.translated_text: than to please oneself with wealth obtained from wicked people. // 68

body.text:
varaṃ vibhavahīnena prāṇais santarpitoanalaḥ
nopacāraparibhraṣṭaḥ kṛpaṇo 'bhyarthitojanaḥ || 69 || ]
body.translated_text: Better that one bereft of wealth feed the fire with his own vital breaths, than that one whose decorum has been destroyed beg from a miserable person. // 69]

body.text:
athaivaṃ gate kenopāyena jīvitaṃ syāt |
kiṃ cauryeṇa |
tad api parasvādānaṃ kaṣṭataram |
yatkāraṇam !
body.translated_text: Now, things being thus, by what means might there be a livelihood? What about theft? That too — taking another's property — is even more wretched. The reason:

body.text:
[ varaṃ yuktaṃ maunaṃ na ca vacanam uktaṃ yad anṛtaṃ
varaṃ mṛtyuś ślāghyo na ca parakalatrābhigamanam |
varaṃ prāṇatyāgo na ca piśunavakyeṣv abhiratir
varaṃ bhikṣārthitvaṃ na ca paradhanāsvādam asakṛt || 70 || ]
body.translated_text: [Better well-employed silence than a word spoken that is false; better a praiseworthy death than approaching another's wife; better the relinquishing of life than delight in the words of a slanderer; better begging than repeatedly savoring another's wealth. // 70]

body.text:
tad arthitve 'pi hi puruṣasya dhruvo 'vamānaḥ |
katham |
body.translated_text: So, even in begging, dishonor is certain for a man. How so?

body.text:
[ ākāraparivṛttis tu buddheḥ paribhavaḥ punaḥ |
āśāhānir ivārthitvaṃ parāsutvam ivāparam || 71 || ]
body.translated_text: [The distortion of one's demeanor, then the insult to one's intelligence, the destruction of hope — begging is like another kind of death. // 71]

body.text:
atha kiṃ parapiṇḍenātmānaṃ yāpayāmi |
kaṣṭaṃ bhoḥ |
tad api dvitīyaṃ mṛtyudvāram |
[ rogī cirapravāsī parānnabhojī parāvasathaśāyī |
yaj jīvati tan maraṇaṃ so 'sya viśrāmaḥ || 72 || ]
body.translated_text: Now, shall I sustain myself by another's food? Wretched, indeed! That too is a second gateway to death. [One who is sick, one on a long journey, one who eats another's food, one who sleeps in another's dwelling — what living he does is [itself] death; that [death] is his rest. // 72]

body.text: api ca |
body.translated_text: Moreover:

body.text:
[ jātaḥ kule mahati mānadhanāvaliptas
sammānanābhyudayakāla iva praharṣī |
tac cheṣapiṇḍam api nāma nṛpasya bhuṅkte
yas sārameya iva kaṣṭataraṃ kim anyat || 73 || ]
body.translated_text: [Born in a great family, puffed up with pride of honor, glad as if the time of increase in esteem had come — yet he eats even the leftover morsels of a king! Like a dog — what could be more wretched? // 73

body.text:
[ āśāviplutacetaso 'bhilaṣitāl lābhād alābho varas
tasyālābhanirākṛtā hi tanutām āpadyate prārthanā |
iṣṭāvāptisamudbhavas tu sutarāṃ harṣaḥ pramāthī dhṛtes
setor bhaṅga ivāmbhasāṃ vivaśatāṃ vegena vistāryate || 74 || ]
body.translated_text: For one whose mind is agitated by hope, non-attainment is better than attainment of the desired object; for non-attainment diminishes and makes slender the desire. But the joy born of obtaining the desired object, being exceedingly maddening of steadfastness, is spread by its force into helplessness, like the breaking of a dam [releases] waters. // 74]

body.text: api ca |
body.translated_text: Moreover:

children.text: [ tiryakpātitacakṣuṣāṃ smayavatām ucchaiḥ kṛtaikabhruvām
children.translated_text: [Of the wealthy, with eyes cast sideways, with smiles of condescension, with a single eyebrow raised,

children.text: āḍhyānām avalepatuṅgaśirasāṃ śrutvā giro dāruṇāḥ |
children.translated_text: with heads held high in the pride of arrogance — having heard their cruel words,

children.text: kiṃ sadyas sphuṭanaṃ prayuktam urasas sevākṛtām arthinām
children.translated_text: does the chest of those who serve them and beg from them

children.text: antas tad yadi varjasāradṛḍhayā nālipyate tṛṣṇayā || 75 ||
children.translated_text: not instantly burst — unless it is bound by a craving as hard as diamond? // 75

body.text:
dīnā dīnamukhair yadi svaśiśukair ākṛṣṭacīrāmbarā
krośadbhiḥ kṣudhitair nirannapiṭhirā dṛśyate no gehinī |
yācñabhaṅgabhayena gadgadagalaproccāritārdhākṣaraṃ
ko dehīti vadet svadagdhajaṭharasyārthe manasvī pumān || 76 || ]
body.translated_text: If the pitiful wife, with her little children — their faces wretched, tugging at her torn garments, crying with hunger, her food-vessels empty — is to be seen at home, what self-respecting man would say 'Give!' in a voice stammering with fear of refusal, half-formed syllables choking in his throat, for the sake of his own wretched belly? // 76]

body.text:
tan nissvateyam anekaprakāraṃ maraṇam |
atha cet tad eva dhanam ātmīkaromi |
mayā tu tayor durātmanor upadhānīkṛtā dṛṣṭapūrvās te dīnārās
sthagitāḥ |
evaṃ ca sampradhārya gato 'haṃ tam uddeśam |
atha tāv anyamanaskau matvā sañjighṛkṣur aham upaśliṣṭaḥ |
dṣṭvā ca māṃ bṛhatsphig laguḍenātāḍayat |
aham api mumūrṣuḥ kathamapi nivṛttaḥ |
punar api cirād baddhāśas samāśvasya dīnārāntikam upaśliṣṭas
tena nirdayenaivaṃ śirasy abhihataḥ ! yenādyāpi svapnagatānām api
tādṛśānām udvije |
paśya cemaṃ tatkālakṛtaṃ śirasi me vraṇam |
sādhu cedam ucyate |
body.translated_text: So, for one without wealth, death [takes] many forms. Now then, if I make that very wealth my own... But I have seen those <s>dīnāras</s> before — they were placed as a pillow by those two wicked ones, [and then] hidden. Having thus deliberated, I went to that spot. Thinking those two were inattentive, I crept close, wishing to seize [the gold]. And seeing me, <s>Bṛhatsphig</s> (Big-buttocks) struck me with a club. Even so, I, wishing to die, somehow withdrew. Again, after a long time, having rallied my bound hopes, I crept close to the <s>dīnāras</s> — and was struck on the head so mercilessly by that cruel one that even now I tremble at [the mere thought of] such ones even in a dream! See this wound on my head made at that time. Well has it been said:

body.text:
[ sarvaprāṇavināśasaṃśayakarīṃ prāpyāpadaṃ dustarāṃ
pratyāsannabhayo na vetti vidhuraṃ svaṃ jīvitaṃ kāṅkṣati |
uttīrṇas tu tato dhanārtham aparāṃ bhūyo viśaty āpadaṃ
prāṇānāṃ ca dhanasya sādhanadhiyām anyonyahetuḥ paṇaḥ || 77 || ]
so 'haṃ bahu vicintyāstāṃ dhanam etan mameti nivṛttas
tṛṣṇātaḥ |
suṣṭu cedam ucyate |
body.translated_text:
['Having encountered a calamity hard to cross, which causes uncertainty about the destruction of all life, the one near danger does not know his own wretched life, yet clings to it. But having escaped from it, for the sake of wealth he enters yet another calamity — the wager of lives, wealth, and scheming minds is one of mutual causation. || 77 ||']
Thus I, having pondered much, said 'Let this wealth remain [where it is]' and turned away from craving. And this is well said:

children.text: [ jñānaṃ cakṣur nedaṃ śīlaṃ kulaputratā na kulajanma |
children.translated_text: ['Knowledge is the eye, not this [physical one]; virtue is noble birth, not birth in a [high] family;

children.text: santoṣaś ca samṛddhiḥ pāṇḍityam avāryavinivṛttiḥ || 78 ||
children.translated_text: contentment is prosperity; scholarship is cessation from what is hard to resist. || 78 ||

children.text: sarvās sampattayas tasya santuṣṭaṃ yasya mānasam |
children.translated_text: All riches belong to him whose mind is content;

children.text: upānadgūḍhapādasya sarvā carmāvṛtaiva bhūḥ || 79 ||
children.translated_text: for one whose foot is covered by a sandal, the entire earth is as if covered in leather. || 79 ||

children.text: na yojanaśataṃ dūraṃ vāhyamānasya tṛṣṇayā |
children.translated_text: A hundred <s>yojanas</s> is not far for one driven by craving;

children.text: sant.uṣṭasya karaprāpte 'py arthe bhavati nādaraḥ || 80 ||
children.translated_text: for the contented one, there is no interest even in wealth within arm's reach. || 80 ||

body.text:
sarpāḥ pibanti pavanaṃ na ca durbalās te
parṇais tṛṇair vanagajā balino bhavanti |
mūlaiḥ phalair munivarāḥ kṣapayanti kālaṃ
santoṣa eva mahatāṃ paramā vibhūtiḥ || 81 || ]
body.translated_text: Serpents drink wind and are not weak for it; forest elephants become mighty on leaves and grass; great sages pass their time on roots and fruits — contentment alone is the supreme wealth of the great. || 81 ||']

body.text: tat sarvathāsādhye 'rthe pariccheda eva śreyān |
body.translated_text: Therefore, when the goal is altogether unattainable, renunciation alone is the better course.

body.text:
[ dāridryasya parā mūrtir yācñā na draviṇālpatā |
jaradgavadhanaś śambhus tathāpi parameśvaraḥ || 82 || ]
body.translated_text: ['The supreme form of poverty is begging, not the scarcity of wealth. <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva), whose wealth is a worn-out bull, is nevertheless the Supreme Lord. || 82 ||']

body.text: tathā ca |
body.translated_text: And also:

children.text: [ ko dharmo bhūtadayā kiṃ saukhyam arogatā jantoḥ |
children.translated_text: ['What is <s>dharma</s>? Compassion for beings. What is happiness? Freedom from disease for a creature.

children.text: kas snehas sadbhāvaḥ kiṃ pāṇḍityaṃ paricchedaḥ || 83 ||
children.translated_text: What is affection? Sincerity. What is scholarship? Discernment. || 83 ||

body.text:

body.translated_text: There is [a story]. In a certain place, there lived a weaver named <s>Somilaka</s>. Whatever he earned did not increase beyond his daily expenses. Having become dejected, he went to another country. There, with great toil, within three years he earned a hundred <s>dīnāras</s> — and set out for his own country. Halfway, at the approach of twilight, having reached a banyan tree in the midst of a forest, he thought: 'Where shall I now go, being very far from the village?' So he decided: 'I shall climb this very banyan tree and spend the night.' Having resolved thus, he did so. At midnight, he saw as if in a dream two men of great stature, of divine appearance, their eyes reddened with anger, who had come to his presence. One of them said: 'O <s>Vaṅkālaka</s>! Is this how it is? I have warned you many times before that nothing should be given to this <s>Somilaka</s> beyond his food and drink. He now has a hundred <s>dīnāras</s>. Quickly take them away!' Then that other one said: 'As you command, lord. I shall do so.' Having heard this, he awoke, and — he did not see the hundred <s>dīnāras</s>! With a dejected heart, he thought: 'Alas! What is this? How have I been cheated here by some spirit? What shall I do now by going home? Let me turn back from here and, having obtained wealth again, go.' Thinking thus, when the night was past, he once again reached the city and, setting his mind on earning wealth, within some time earned fifty <s>dīnāras</s> and again set out on the same road toward his own country. But, as if driven by fate, he could not obtain more, nor could he travel by another road. He was led to that very spot — and when the sun was setting, he reached that very banyan tree. He thought: 'Alas! What is this that the ill-fated one has begun? That same <s>rākṣasa</s> in the form of the banyan [is here] again.' Thus pondering, as he fell asleep, he again saw those same two men. One of them said: 'O <s>Vaṅkāla</s>! <s>Somilaka</s> has fifty <s>dīnāras</s>. That is not proper.' Then the other said: 'Consider them taken.' <s>Somilaka</s>, having awoken, did not see them — they had been taken. Then, filled with dejection, he said: 'What use is my life? What is this turn of events? For what reason does someone take away my wealth earned through toil — I do not understand. I shall give up my life.' Thinking thus, fasting, he remained there, until within a few days he saw a man of divine form. That one said: 'O <s>Somilaka</s>! I am <s>Dhanada</s> (the giver of wealth). I do not give wealth to anyone for whom it is not destined. And so —'

body.translated_text: 'Nevertheless, through the conjunction of fate and human effort, wealth arises. A person acts; fate bears fruit.' 'Here, I, who was devoted to effort, have been seen by you. My sight is never in vain. What shall I do for you?' He [<s>Somilaka</s>] petitioned: 'Give me wealth.' <s>Dhanada</s> (the wealth-giver), laughing, said: 'Fool! What use is that? Enjoyment is what matters here. Go! In this very place, observe two merchants. One is wealthy; the other enjoys [his wealth]. Having seen the two, whichever of them you prefer — such you shall become.' Having said this, he vanished. <s>Somilaka</s> too, at dawn, entering that city, came upon a caravan-leader named <s>Dhanagupta</s> (Wealth-protector). There, though rebuked, he somehow entered the house and lay down on the veranda. That merchant too, having spent the evening, at nightfall took only a meager meal. He also gave <s>Somilaka</s> only a meager meal. Then that weaver, having spread <s>kuśa</s> grass, lying down on the ground, fell asleep and saw those same two persons [in a dream]. One of them said: 'O <s>Vaṅkāla</s>! <s>Dhanagupta</s>, by giving the weaver a meal today, has incurred double the expenditure.' 'I keep a careful account of everything. Nothing has been allotted to this one except for storage — neither a gift nor a meal. I shall settle accounts in the morning.' Having heard this, he awoke. <s>Dhanagupta</s> too, in the morning, fell gravely ill with cholera, and being afflicted by perspiration, hot water, drinks, and such treatments, went without food. Then that weaver, at dawn, prompted by fate, thought: 'What use is wealth of this kind? Nature is hard to abandon.' Then <s>Somilaka</s> went to the second one, <s>Bhogavarman</s> (Enjoyment-protector), who was of a spending disposition. By him, <s>Somilaka</s> was honored with great food, drink, and such, and likewise, sleeping at night in a great bed, well-furnished and well-prepared, he saw those same two persons. One of them said: 'Good <s>Vaṅkāla</s>! <s>Bhogavarman</s> has done well by honoring the guest <s>Somilaka</s>. Therefore, even more of the increasing wealth must be given to him for expenditure and enjoyment.' He [the other] replied: 'So be it.' <s>Somilaka</s>, having awakened, thought: 'May enjoyments such as this be mine! What use is wealth that is merely a name?' And so he resolved.

body.translated_text: There is [a story]. I was once born as a <s>priyaka</s> deer in the region of <s>Śāligrāma</s> on the banks of the <s>Yamunā</s>. We are of six species. And so: the <s>camūra</s>, <s>kadalī</s>, <s>kandalī</s>, <s>priyaka</s>, and <s>eṇaka</s> — these are the five praised deer species. By the grace of their mother's milk, they know two gaits: the upward [leap] and the straight [run]. They cannot be caught by hunters. I, being of the <s>priyaka</s> species, am beloved of humans and close my eyes only after a long time. It being so, when my mother had gone away, I, still a fawn, was captured by hunters. Nourished on human women's milk, while I lived in that household, my mother roamed with her own herd. She said: 'Alas, fate! I am without a son — where is my child?' Having heard this, I resolved: 'What are these hunters to me? Between a natural companion and an artificial one, the natural companion is greater.' Then I freely departed from the hunter's dwelling. Then, having come from the hunter — with fearful, startled eyes — I reached my mother. She was overjoyed. When asked 'What is this wonder?', [I replied that I was] nourished on human breast-milk. Because of that, I, a six-month-old fawn, surpassed my own herd. Through my superior speed, outpacing the deer, I would wait for those behind to arrive. We have two gaits: upward and straight. Of these, due to deprivation of my mother's milk, I knew only the straight one, not the upward. Then once, not seeing the deer as they moved, my heart distressed, I looked [wondering] 'Where have they gone?' I saw them — knowing the upward gait, they had leaped over the net and gone ahead. body.translated_text: I, not knowing the upward gait due to the deficiency of that 'medicine' called [mother's] milk, went forward by the straight gait and became entangled in the net. Then wicked hunters, having captured me alive, brought me to a prince for his amusement. He too, upon seeing me, was extremely pleased and honored the hunters with a reward. He tended me with care — body-massage, bathing, feeding, incense, ornaments, garments, and extraordinary food preparations: smooth, tender, rich, mixed with raw sugar, jaggery, pomegranate, and the four spices, along with other delicacies — and thus he nourished me. Then, passed from hand to hand among the women of the inner quarters and the princes, tormented out of curiosity by pulling of neck, eyes, hands, feet, and ears, and harassed by the competing attention of the royal ladies — I suffered greatly. I thought: 'What use is gold that hurts the ears? Alas! When shall I reach that forest?' santāpitahṛdayas samantād avalokayan mām apaśyat |
ahaṃ ca lubdhakair mānuṣīṃ vācaṃ śikṣita āsam |
dṛṣṭvā ca māṃ mānuṣeṇevānena mṛgenābhihitam ! vinaṣṭo 'smīti
matvā paramāvegaṃ gataḥ |

paramasattvādhiṣṭhita iva mahad asvāsthyam āpede |
tatas sarvābhiṣagbhūtatantrikān mahatyā arthamātrayā jvaraparītaḥ
prārthitavān ! evaṃ cābravīt |
yo mamaitāṃ rujam apanayati ! tasyāham akṛśāṃ pūjāṃ
kariṣyāmīti |
aham api tatrāsamīkṣitakāriṇā janena laguḍeṣṭakādibhir
druhyamāṇaḥ kenāpi sādhunāvacchannaḥ |
kim anena kṛtam iti |
atha mamāyuśśeṣatayā tenāryeṇa sarvalakṣaṇavidā vijñāpito
rājaputraḥ |
avimarśapareṇa lokenemām avasthāṃ prāpitastvam |
punar api tenāryeṇokto yathā |
priyako nāmaiṣa mṛgo mānuṣīṃ vācaṃ jānāti |
naiṣa mānuṣaḥ |
bhadra ! anena prāvṛṭkālameghaśabdapratibodhitacittena
svayūthyānusmaraṇautsukyād abhihitam |
vātavṛsṭyavadhūtasyeti |
kim atra citram |
prāyeṇa pakṣiṇaḥ paśavaś ca bhayāhāramaithunamātravedino
bhavanti ! ity adhigatam eva devena |
ato 'yam amānuṣaḥ |
tathā ca |
body.translated_text: While I was uttering this, the prince, being young and of unsteady mind, having heard this much, was terrified and said to the doorkeeper: 'Who said this?' With an anguished heart, looking about on all sides, he saw me. Now I had been taught human speech by the hunters. Seeing me, he thought 'This deer has spoken in human language — I am ruined!' and became extremely agitated. Then, somehow stammering, he went outside and was overcome by a great fit of illness, as if possessed by a supreme being. Thereupon, in a fever, he summoned all physicians, exorcists, and tantric specialists with a great reward, and said: 'Whoever removes this affliction of mine — to him I shall offer no small honor.' Meanwhile, I too was assailed with sticks, bricks, and such by thoughtless people, until some good man shielded me: 'What has this one done?' Then, because I had some life remaining, that noble man, versed in all the marks [of animals], informed the prince: 'You have been brought to this condition by thoughtless people. Moreover,' that noble one said: 'This is a deer of the <s>priyaka</s> species that knows human speech. He is not a human. Good sir, this one, his heart stirred by the sound of thunder-clouds in the rainy season, spoke out of longing to remember his herd-mates: "When will it come to pass — tossed by wind and rain..." What is strange about this? It is well known to your lordship that birds and animals generally know only fear, food, and mating.' Therefore, this is not a human. And thus —

children.translated_text: 'With whomever one dwells, and whomever one serves,

children.text: yādṛg icchec ca bhavituṃ tādṛg bhavati pūruṣaḥ || 151 ||
children.translated_text: and whatever one wishes to become — such indeed does a person become.'

body.text:
hīyate hi naras tāta hīnais saha samāgamāt |
samaiś ca samatām eti viśiṣṭaiś ca viśiṣṭatām || 152 || ]
body.translated_text: 'A man diminishes, dear one, from association with the low; he becomes equal through association with equals; and he attains distinction through association with the distinguished.'

tat ! deva ! manuṣyasamparkāt priyakajātivaśāc ca mānuṣīṃ vācaṃ
dadātīti sammānitaḥ |
tathā ca |
body.translated_text: 'Therefore, your highness, through contact with humans and by the nature of the <s>priyaka</s> species, he produces human speech.' And he was honored. And thus —

 || 153 || ]

body.translated_text: So [it is]. What is unrelated here as a cause of fever? Moreover —

body.text:
[ mantrāṇāṃ parato nāsti bījam uccaraṇaṃ tathā |
asambaddhapralāpā na kāryaṃ sādhayituṃ kṣamāh || 154 || ]
body.translated_text: 'There is no seed of <s>mantras</s> (sacred formulas) apart from proper pronunciation. Incoherent babbling is not capable of accomplishing any purpose.'

body.translated_text: And thus —

body.text:
[ śaṅkhaḥ kadalyāṃ kadalī ca bheryāṃ
tasyāṃ ca bheryāṃ sumahad vimānam |
tacchaṅkhabherīkadalīvimānam
unmattaśaṅkāpratimaṃ babhūva || 155 || ]
body.translated_text: 'A conch in a plantain tree, and a plantain in a drum, and in that drum a great aerial chariot — that assemblage of conch, drum, plantain, and chariot was like the fancy of a madman.'

body.text:
tat kva śaṅkaḥ ! kva kadalī ! kva bherī ! kva vimānam iti |
tadvidham idam asambaddhatayā tvayy āgatam |
tac ca śrutvāpagatavikāro rājaputraḥ pūrvaprakṛtim āpannaḥ |
vicārya tasyāryasya prajñāvibhavaṃ tato mahatīṃ pūjāṃ kṛtvā
mantrisamīpavartī mantritve kṛtaḥ |
māṃ cāpanīyābhyajya prabhūtenāmbhasā prakṣālitaśarīraṃ
kṛtvārakṣipuruṣādhiṣṭhitaṃ tatraiva vane pratimuktavān |
tat kiṃ bahunā ! anubhūtabandhano 'py ahaṃ niyativaśāt punar
baddha iti |
body.translated_text: 'So where is the conch? Where is the banana tree? Where is the drum? Where is the aerial chariot?' — in this manner, this incoherent [speech] has come upon you. And hearing that, the prince, his agitation removed, returned to his former nature. Having recognized the wisdom and intelligence of that noble man, and having done him great honor, he appointed him as a minister in the company of [his other] ministers. And having removed me [from the post], he had my body washed with abundant water, anointed me, and placed me — guarded by protectors — back in that very forest, setting me free. So what more is there to say? Though I experienced captivity, by the force of destiny I have been captured again.
